reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / oculoplastic and maxillofacial references
clinicalPearls: A fracture of the orbital wall, most often the floor or medial wall, from blunt trauma without fracture of the orbital rim
Features include periorbital bruising, diplopia, restricted eye movements (especially vertical), enophthalmos and infraorbital numbness
Vertical diplopia from inferior rectus tethering is typical, and pain or nausea on upgaze suggests muscle entrapment
In children a white-eyed blowout fracture with muscle entrapment and marked oculocardiac reflex is a surgical emergency
CT of the orbit defines the fracture and any herniated or entrapped tissue
Many fractures are managed conservatively, with surgery for significant entrapment, enophthalmos or persistent diplopia
reference.pathophysiology: An orbital blowout fracture occurs when blunt force raises intra-orbital pressure or buckles the orbital walls, fracturing the thin floor or medial wall while sparing the sturdier rim. Orbital fat and the inferior rectus or its surrounding tissue can prolapse or become entrapped in the fracture, causing restricted motility and diplopia, while loss of orbital volume support leads to enophthalmos. Injury to the infraorbital nerve produces cheek and upper-lip numbness. In children the more elastic bone can snap shut and trap muscle (a trapdoor mechanism), causing ischaemia and a marked oculocardiac reflex.
additionalDifferentials: Orbital rim or complex facial fracture
Traumatic extraocular muscle palsy without entrapment
Globe rupture or other ocular trauma
Orbital cellulitis (if delayed presentation with swelling)
additionalInvestigations: CT of the orbits and facial bones
Full ophthalmic assessment to exclude globe injury
Assessment of ocular motility, diplopia and enophthalmos
Monitoring for the oculocardiac reflex, especially in children
redFlags: White-eyed blowout fracture with entrapment and bradycardia in a child (surgical emergency)
Signs of globe rupture or retrobulbar haemorrhage with visual loss
A relative afferent pupillary defect indicating optic nerve injury
reference.prognosis: Many blowout fractures do well with conservative care and resolution of early diplopia; timely surgery for entrapment or significant volume change gives good outcomes, whereas delayed treatment of paediatric entrapment risks permanent motility problems.
pitfalls: Missing a paediatric trapdoor entrapment that needs urgent surgery
Attributing early diplopia solely to swelling and not reassessing
Failing to warn against nose-blowing, which can cause orbital emphysema
